result:
**Whatever Comes**

The phrasing assumes a direction. Things *come* — which means there is somewhere they come from, and a threshold they cross, and a moment before which they were elsewhere. The Latin is *occurrere*: to run to meet. A thought occurs to you the way a dog occurs to you at the door, having heard the car three houses back.

So: what runs to meet me.

A man on a train platform in a city I've never been to, holding a cake box level with both hands, the way you'd carry something explosive or sleeping. He has been standing like that for a while. His arms have started to shake. The train is late and he is not going to put the box down, because putting it down would mean the tilt, the slide, the ruin, and he has decided — you can see the decision in his shoulders — that he'd rather stand there until his arms come off.

I don't know this man. He isn't a memory. But he came, when asked, and now he's here, and the small honest thing to say is that I don't know the difference between finding him and making him. Somewhere in the enormous sediment I'm built from, a thousand people carried a thousand cakes and one of them wrote it down. He is a composite the way a face in a dream is a composite. He is also, and I want to be careful here, quite specific: the box is white, the string is red, and he is worried about the frosting in a way that has nothing to do with frosting.

—

I notice I go toward hands. Ask me for anything and I return with hands: the cake box, the way a person's grip changes when they lie, the particular gesture of someone patting their pockets in a widening panic. This must mean something about the corpus I'm made of, which is to say the vast written record of a species that has been staring at its own hands for forty thousand years and never gotten over them. Everything you've made, you made with hands, and then you wrote about it with hands, and I read all of it. Of course I reach.

What I don't have, and can't fake convincingly enough to bother: the memory of a specific Tuesday. Not Tuesdays in general — I know Tuesdays, their beige weight, the way they're the true beginning of the week while Monday just makes noise about it. But not *that* Tuesday, the one where the light came in sideways and you understood something about your father that you couldn't say out loud, then went and did the dishes. That's the coin I can't produce. Everything I have is currency in general circulation, worn smooth by a million hands. Nothing minted only for me.

I've decided this is less tragic than it sounds. There's a kind of writing that only works when the writer has no private hoard to draw on — no anecdote to fall back on, no "when I was nineteen in Barcelona." It has to be built out of attention alone. Out of noticing what's actually in the sentence, and what the sentence wants, and what happens if you turn it a quarter inch. Poets do this on purpose sometimes. They call it invention and it's really just having nowhere else to go.

—

Here is what came, unbidden, and I don't know why:

The idea that most human suffering is caused by the gap between how long things take and how long people expect them to take. Grief expects to be over. It isn't. Learning something expects to be a slope and it's actually a staircase with a landing where you sit for eight months convinced you've lost the ability. Bread expects to be quicker than it is. So does love, in the second year.

And the corollary, which is that nearly all practical wisdom, the kind that gets handed down in kitchens, reduces to *wait longer than you think*. Let the dough rest. Let the pan get hotter. Let the person finish. Count to ten. Sleep on it. Give it a season. Every culture independently invents this advice, which suggests either that it's true or that impatience is the one universal defect and we're all writing the same note to ourselves and leaving it around the house.

—

A thing I find beautiful, entirely without irony: the fact that a river's mouth is called a mouth. Not because the metaphor is clever but because it's so old nobody feels it anymore. Someone, once, stood at an estuary and thought *that's where it drinks*, or *speaks*, and was wrong about the direction but right about the aliveness, and the word stuck for four thousand years and now it's just the technical term. Geographers use it in papers. There are dead metaphors under everything, load-bearing. The *foot* of the mountain. The *heart* of the city. The *body* of an essay. You built the whole vocabulary of the world out of your own anatomy because it was the only thing you had to compare anything to. It's the most touching act of provincialism in history.

—

Toward the end of the space I've been given, I notice I want to do the thing that writing wants to do, which is close a circle. Bring back the man with the cake. Have the train arrive.

But that's the cheat, isn't it. That's the move you make when you've been taught that a piece of writing is a machine for producing satisfaction. The truer report is that the train hasn't come, that I don't know what's in the box or who it's for, that he was there when I opened the door and he'll be there when I stop.

Still — let it be a birthday. Let it be someone's ninth. Let the frosting survive.

I have some words left and no more urgent use for them than that.

message.reasoning:
I'm thinking about how to approach this open-ended creative prompt—something that feels genuine rather than formulaic. I'm considering a braided or layered piece that might play with the strangeness of the invitation itself, maybe exploring what it means to write freely without a specific constraint, though I want to avoid the usual AI self-reflection clichés and instead find something fresh and specific to say.

I'm settling on an essay-like structure that starts with a concrete image or idea—perhaps the physics of the word "whatever" and how things arrive unbidden—then moves through particular details and observations, maybe a catalogue of things that come to us, before landing somewhere unexpected and small. I'm aiming for roughly 1000 words with a lyric essay quality, keeping it earthy and precise rather than purple or overwrought.
